topics.topic: Gender and articles: el, la, un, una
topics.explain: Every Spanish noun is masculine or feminine. Most nouns in -o are masculine (el libro) and most in -a are feminine (la mesa); learn the rest with their article (el café, la leche). 'The' = el/la (plural los/las); 'a/an' = un/una (some = unos/unas). Watch out: some break the pattern: el día, la mano.
examples: El libro está en la mesa.
The book is on the table.
Hay un café y una naranja.
There is a coffee and an orange.

questions.why: 'Mano' is feminine (la mano) even though it ends in -o. It is one of the exceptions you must learn with its article.
'Mesa' is feminine, so 'una mesa'. Libro is masculine (un libro), and a plural noun needs a plural article (los libros).

topics.explain: Add -s to nouns ending in a vowel (casa → casas) and -es after a consonant (flor → flores). Adjectives usually go after the noun and match it in gender and number: un paraguas rojo, una manzana roja, las uvas rojas. Adjectives in -e or a consonant change only for number: grande/grandes, azul/azules. Watch out: not 'las rojas uvas' or 'las uvas rojo'.
examples: Mi hermana tiene el pelo largo y negro.
My sister has long black hair.
Las uvas rojas son muy ricas.
The red grapes are very tasty.

questions.why: 'Las flores' is feminine plural, so the adjective is feminine plural: bonitas.
Article, noun and adjective all agree (feminine plural), and the adjective follows the noun: las manzanas rojas.

topics.explain: Drop -ar, -er or -ir and add an ending for the subject. hablar: hablo, hablas, habla, hablamos, habláis, hablan. comer: como, comes, come, comemos, coméis, comen. vivir: vivo, vives, vive, vivimos, vivís, viven. Watch out: usted takes the él/ella form and ustedes the ellos form; subject pronouns are usually left out.
examples: Do you eat bread for breakfast?

questions.why: 'Mis amigos' = ellos, so the ending is -en: viven.
-ar verbs take -amos for nosotros in the present: trabajamos. Trabajan is ellos/ustedes, trabajáis is vosotros, and trabajemos is the subjunctive, which does not fit a plain statement.

topics.explain: 'Ser' (to be) is irregular: soy, eres, es, somos, sois, son. Use it for identity and lasting traits: name, origin, nationality, job, what someone is like, plus days and time: Soy Ana, Es de Chile, Es alto. Watch out: with jobs Spanish drops 'a/an' (Soy profesora), and feelings and location take estar instead.
examples: Soy de México y soy estudiante.
I am from Mexico and I am a student.

questions.why: Origin uses ser, and the nosotros form is 'somos'.

questions.q: How do you say 'She is a doctor'?
questions.why: Jobs use ser and normally no article: Ella es médica.

topics.topic: Possessive adjectives: mi, tu, su, nuestro
topics.explain: Possessives go before the noun: mi (my), tu (your), su (his/her/their, or your formal), nuestro/nuestra (our). They add -s before plural nouns: mis libros, tus amigas. Only nuestro (and vuestro) also change for gender: nuestra casa. Watch out: they agree with the thing owned, not the owner. 'Tu' (your) has no accent; 'tú' (you) does.
examples: Mi casa está cerca de tu escuela.
My house is near your school.

questions.q: Complete: Ana y yo vivimos con ___ abuela. (our)
questions.why: 'Our' agrees with the thing owned: abuela is feminine singular, so 'nuestra'.
Before a plural noun, 'mi' becomes 'mis'; the noun stays plural: mis libros.

topics.topic: Stem-changing verbs: e → ie, o → ue
topics.explain: Some verbs change a vowel in the stem: querer → quiero, poder → puedo, costar → cuesta, sentarse → me siento. The change appears in every present form except nosotros and vosotros: queremos, podemos. The endings stay regular. Watch out: learners often say 'quero' or 'podo', so learn these verbs with their yo form.
examples: Queremos ir a la playa, pero no podemos.
We want to go to the beach, but we can't.

questions.q: Complete: Yo ___ un café, por favor. (querer)
questions.why: Querer changes e → ie in the yo form: quiero.
Nosotros forms keep the original stem: podemos (no o → ue change). Pueden is ellos/ustedes, and podamos is the subjunctive, which does not fit a plain statement.
